claim: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been associated with juvenile experience-dependent primary visual cortex (V1) plasticity.
source: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been associated with juvenile experience-dependent primary visual cortex (V1) plasticity, yet little is known about their role in this process in the adult V1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about MMPs and juvenile V1 plasticity.

claim: Little is known about the role of MMPs in adult V1 plasticity.
source: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been associated with juvenile experience-dependent primary visual cortex (V1) plasticity, yet little is known about their role in this process in the adult V1.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Activation of MMPs is a crucial step facilitating structural changes in a healthy brain.
source: Activation of MMPs is a crucial step facilitating structural changes in a healthy brain; however, upon brain injury, upregulated MMPs promote the spread of a lesion and impair recovery.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Upon brain injury, upregulated MMPs promote the spread of a lesion and impair recovery.
source: Activation of MMPs is a crucial step facilitating structural changes in a healthy brain; however, upon brain injury, upregulated MMPs promote the spread of a lesion and impair recovery.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: 7-day application of MMP-inhibitor prevented visual plasticity in healthy adult animals.
source: In healthy animals, 7-day application of MMP-inhibitor prevented visual plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Treatment with MMP-inhibitor once but not twice following stroke rescued plasticity.
source: Additionally, treatment with MMP-inhibitor once but not twice following stroke rescued plasticity, normally lost under these conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: An optimal level of MMP-activity is crucial for adult visual plasticity to occur.

evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the experimental results.

claim: The primary visual cortex (V1) is a widely used model region for studying sensory plasticity in young vs. adult brains.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, V1 consists of a monocular and a binocular zone.
source: In mammals, V1 consists of a monocular and a binocular zone; neurons in the binocular zone respond to stimulation of both eyes but are dominated by the contralateral eye in rodents (Dräger, 1975; 1978).
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in the binocular zone respond to stimulation of both eyes but are dominated by the contralateral eye in rodents.
source: In mammals, V1 consists of a monocular and a binocular zone; neurons in the binocular zone respond to stimulation of both eyes but are dominated by the contralateral eye in rodents (Dräger, 1975; 1978).

claim: Ocular dominance (OD) can be modified in an experience-dependent manner by depriving one eye of pattern vision for several days.
source: This ocular dominance (OD) can be modified in an experience-dependent manner, by depriving one eye of pattern vision for several days (known as monocular deprivation or MD), as originally observed by Wiesel and Hubel more than 50 years ago (Wiesel and Hubel, 1965).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OD-plasticity has become one of the major paradigms for studying cortical plasticity.
source: OD-plasticity has become one of the major paradigms for studying cortical plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In standard-cage raised mice, OD-plasticity in binocular V1 is most pronounced in 4-week-old animals.
source: In standard-cage raised mice, OD-plasticity in binocular V1 is most pronounced in 4-week-old animals; reduced, yet present, in early adulthood; and absent in animals older than 110 days of age (Lehmann and Löwel, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: OD-plasticity is reduced, yet present, in early adulthood in standard-cage raised mice.

claim: OD-plasticity is absent in standard-cage raised mice older than 110 days of age.

claim: In 4-week-old mice, 3-4 days of MD are sufficient to induce a significant OD-shift towards the open eye.
source: In 4-week-old mice, 3-4 days of MD are sufficient to induce a significant OD-shift towards the open eye (juvenile OD-plasticity), while 7 days of MD are needed in 3-month-old animals (adult OD-plasticity) (Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Sawtell et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Sato and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 7 days of MD are needed to induce OD-plasticity in 3-month-old animals.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Molecular mechanisms underlying 'juvenile' and 'adult' OD-plasticity are different.
source: Although the experimental paradigm is rather similar, molecular mechanisms underlying 'juvenile' and 'adult' OD-plasticity are different: in juvenile mice, OD-shifts are mostly mediated by reductions in deprived eye responses while adult plasticity is predominantly mediated by an increase in open eye responses in V1 (Hofer et al., 2006; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Levelt and Hübener, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In juvenile mice, OD-shifts are mostly mediated by reductions in deprived eye responses.

claim: Adult plasticity is predominantly mediated by an increase in open eye responses in V1.
